common_name: Japanese Mahonia (Fragrant Winter-Flowering Shade Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Japanese Mahonia is the parent species behind the popular x media hybrids, valued for pendant, lemon-scented winter flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Japanese Mahonia bears bold, holly-like, pinnately compound evergreen foliage and, in late fall through winter, pendant racemes of small, lemon-scented yellow flowers that are among the earliest nectar sources for winter-active pollinators, followed by tart, dusty-blue-black berries that can be used for jelly. Its architectural foliage and off-season bloom give it strong winter garden value when little else is flowering. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes, since it needs little routine shaping.

common_name: Charity Mahonia (Upright Fragrant Winter Flower Spikes)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Charity is a Slieve Donard hybrid bred for tall, upright, fragrant yellow winter flower spikes.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Charity, a classic Slieve Donard nursery hybrid of Mahonia japonica and Mahonia lonicera, bears tall, upright spikes of fragrant yellow flowers in late fall into winter, held above bold, holly-like evergreen foliage, followed by tart blue-black berries usable for jelly or wine. Its architectural form and off-season bloom give it strong winter garden value when little else is flowering. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes.

common_name: Winter Sun Mahonia (Early-Flowering Glossy-Leaf Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Winter Sun is a sister seedling to Charity, flowering earlier with glossy dark foliage.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Winter Sun, a sister seedling to Charity, bears upright spikes of fragrant yellow flowers that open earlier in the fall-to-winter season than most Mahonia x media selections, held above glossy, dark green, holly-like evergreen foliage. Its earlier bloom timing extends the winter flowering window in the shade garden, providing an early nectar source before other Mahonia hybrids open. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes.

common_name: Amber Waves Coral Bells (Ruffled Amber-Gold Foliage Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Amber Waves holds its ruffled amber-gold foliage color best out of the hottest afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; some morning sun deepens the amber-gold foliage color while afternoon shade prevents scorch and fading in hot climates. Amber Waves bears ruffled, wavy-edged leaves in a warm amber-gold that holds color through the growing season, forming a dense mound topped in early summer by airy, wiry stems of tiny white flowers that attract hummingbirds and pollinators. Its bright, ruffled foliage provides season-long color in a shaded border even when not in bloom. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor, and remove old, tattered leaves in late winter.

common_name: Grape Soda Coral Bells (Rounded Deep Purple-Red Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Grape Soda bears rounded, deep purple-red foliage that tolerates heavier shade than most Heuchera cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Grape Soda bears rounded, ruffled leaves in a deep, saturated purple-red that holds its rich color well in shadier sites than many other coral bells cultivars tolerate, forming a dense mound topped in early summer by wiry stems of small white flowers that attract pollinators. Its dark, glossy foliage provides strong color contrast against lighter-leaved shade companions like hostas and ferns. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor, and remove old, tattered leaves in late winter.

common_name: Dolce Key Lime Pie Coral Bells (Chartreuse-Lime Foliage Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Dolce Key Lime Pie bears bright chartreuse-lime foliage with a contrasting red-purple leaf underside.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; some morning sun brightens the chartreuse foliage color while afternoon shade prevents scorch in hot climates. Dolce Key Lime Pie bears bright, glowing chartreuse-lime leaves with a contrasting deep red-purple reverse visible when the ruffled leaf edges curl, forming a dense mound topped in early summer by wiry stems of small white flowers that attract pollinators. Its vivid, citrus-bright color lights up a shaded border and pairs well with darker-leaved companion perennials. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor, and remove old, tattered leaves in late winter.

common_name: Elizabeth Oliver Foamflower (Double Pale Pink Native Foamflower)

planting.note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; Elizabeth Oliver bears unusual double, pale pink flowers on a native foamflower selection that spreads to form a groundcover.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade, the same woodland conditions the native species favors. Elizabeth Oliver bears unusual double, pale pink flower spikes in spring above lobed, softly hairy leaves that often take on bronze-red tones in cooler weather, spreading gently by stolons to form a dense, weed-suppressing native groundcover over time. Its double flower form is a rare trait among foamflower cultivars, giving a fuller, more textured bloom than the typical single-flowered species. Keep soil consistently moist and mulch with leaf litter or shredded bark to mimic its native forest-floor habitat.

common_name: Golden Zebra Heucherella (Gold Foliage with Dark Red Venation)

planting.note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Golden Zebra is a Heuchera-Tiarella hybrid with bold gold foliage marked by dark red central veining.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; some morning sun intensifies the gold foliage color while afternoon shade prevents scorch. Golden Zebra, an intergeneric hybrid between Heuchera and Tiarella, bears deeply lobed gold leaves marked with bold dark red venation radiating from the center, a striking pattern that intensifies through the growing season, topped in late spring by airy spikes of small pinkish-white flowers. Combining the tidy mounding habit of Heuchera with the spreading vigor of Tiarella, it makes an effective, colorful shade groundcover. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor.

common_name: Valley Valentine Pieris (Deep Rose-Red Flowered Evergreen Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Valley Valentine bears unusually deep rose-red flower clusters, among the darkest-colored of any Pieris cultivar.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and winter winds; mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and acidity. Valley Valentine bears cascading clusters of deep rose-red, urn-shaped flowers in late winter to early spring, among the darkest and most saturated flower color of any widely grown Pieris cultivar, opening against glossy, dark evergreen foliage with the reddish-bronze new growth typical of the species. Its intensely colored blooms provide a striking early-season accent when little else in the shade garden is flowering. Water during dry spells and prune lightly after flowering to shape, since Pieris needs little routine pruning.

common_name: Katsura Pieris (Wine-Red New Growth Evergreen Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Katsura bears striking wine-red new growth that matures to green, along with red-tinted flower buds.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and winter winds; mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and acidity. Katsura bears vivid wine-red new growth in spring that gradually matures to dark green, extending its colorful season well beyond the typical spring flush of most Pieris cultivars, and carries red-tinted flower buds through winter that open into cascading clusters of white to pale pink, urn-shaped blooms in late winter to early spring. Its long-lasting foliage color gives it multi-season interest beyond the flower display alone. Water during dry spells and prune lightly after flowering to shape.

common_name: Kew Green Skimmia (Compact Fragrant Male Pollinator Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Kew Green is a compact male Skimmia selection grown chiefly as a fragrant pollinator for female berry-producing cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Kew Green is a compact, rounded male Skimmia selection grown chiefly as a fragrant pollinator for female Skimmia japonica cultivars, producing dense clusters of small, sweetly scented greenish-white flowers in spring above glossy, leathery evergreen foliage. Because it is male it sets no berries itself, but a single Kew Green can pollinate several nearby female plants over a wide radius. Water during dry spells, mulch to maintain acidic, evenly moist soil, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches.

common_name: Carol Mackie Daphne (Variegated Fragrant Pink-Flowered Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; Carol Mackie bears cream-margined variegated leaves and intensely fragrant pale pink spring flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun; Daphne resents disturbance once established, so choose a permanent site and avoid transplanting. Carol Mackie bears blue-green leaves crisply edged in creamy white through the growing season, brightening the shrub even out of bloom, and in mid-spring produces clusters of small, intensely fragrant pale pink flowers that perfume the surrounding garden. Its compact, rounded habit and season-long variegated foliage make it a favorite specimen near an entry or path where its fragrance can be enjoyed up close. Avoid heavy pruning and wet feet, both of which Daphne tolerates poorly; all parts are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Blackberry Wine Corydalis (Deep Wine-Purple Long-Blooming Shade Perennial)

planting.note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Blackberry Wine bears deep wine-purple tubular flowers over blue-green ferny foliage through much of the growing season.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; consistent moisture, especially in summer heat, keeps the plant flowering well. Blackberry Wine bears clusters of deep wine-purple, spurred, tubular flowers held above finely cut, blue-green, ferny foliage, blooming over an unusually long stretch of the growing season from spring into fall rather than the brief spring show typical of many woodland Corydalis species. Its long bloom period and soft, airy foliage texture make it a valuable filler among hostas, ferns, and other shade perennials. Divide congested clumps in spring, and keep soil from drying out during summer to sustain continued flowering.

common_name: Crotonifolia Aucuba (Classic Gold-Speckled Evergreen Laurel)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in shade to deep shade; Crotonifolia is a heavily gold-speckled classic Aucuba cultivar that tolerates some of the deepest shade of any evergreen shrub.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in shade to deep shade; sun causes unattractive yellowing and leaf scorch, so this is one of the best broadleaf evergreens for the darkest corners of the garden. Crotonifolia bears large, glossy, dark green leaves heavily speckled with irregular gold flecks, one of the most boldly variegated Aucuba selections, brightening deep-shade plantings where little else provides year-round color. As a female cultivar it needs a male Aucuba such as 'Mr. Goldstrike' nearby to set the bright red berries that persist through winter. It tolerates salt spray, pollution, and heavy shade under large trees better than nearly any other broadleaf evergreen, needing only occasional pruning to control size.

common_name: Mr. Goldstrike Aucuba (Male Pollinator Gold-Splashed Evergreen Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in shade to deep shade; Mr. Goldstrike is a male Aucuba selection with bold gold-splashed leaves, useful as a pollinator for female berry-bearing cultivars.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in shade to deep shade; sun causes unattractive yellowing and leaf scorch, so this is one of the best broadleaf evergreens for the darkest corners of the garden. Mr. Goldstrike bears large, glossy leaves boldly splashed with gold blotches at the center, and as a male cultivar it produces no berries itself but is essential for pollinating nearby female Aucuba selections such as 'Variegata' or 'Crotonifolia' so they set their showy red winter berries. Its bright, bold foliage provides year-round color in the deepest shade with almost no maintenance. It tolerates salt spray, pollution, and heavy shade under large trees better than nearly any other broadleaf evergreen.

common_name: Sulphur Aucuba (Yellow-Margined Evergreen Laurel)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in shade to deep shade; Sulphur bears dark green leaves margined in sulfur-yellow that matures to creamy white.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in shade to deep shade; sun causes unattractive yellowing and leaf scorch, so this is one of the best broadleaf evergreens for the darkest corners of the garden. Sulphur bears dark green leaves edged with a band of sulfur-yellow that softens to creamy white as the foliage matures, giving a more subtly variegated look than the boldly speckled Aucuba cultivars. As a female selection it needs a male Aucuba such as 'Mr. Goldstrike' nearby to set the bright red berries that persist through winter. It tolerates salt spray, pollution, and heavy shade under large trees better than nearly any other broadleaf evergreen.

common_name: Girard's Rainbow Leucothoe (Pink-Copper New Growth Evergreen Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in consistently moist, deeply acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Girard's Rainbow bears new growth in shades of pink, cream, and copper before maturing to green.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, deeply acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mimicking its native Appalachian stream-bank habitat. Girard's Rainbow emerges each spring in vivid tones of pink, cream, and copper before gradually maturing to glossy green, giving the arching, evergreen shrub a colorful, ever-changing foliage display on top of the fragrant white bell-shaped spring flowers typical of the species. Its variegated new growth makes it more ornamentally striking than the straight species, especially massed under rhododendrons or azaleas. All parts are toxic; spreads slowly by stolons to form a graceful, naturalistic colony.

common_name: Scarlet Beauty Virginia Sweetspire (Cold-Hardy Vivid Fall Color Native Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist to wet, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Scarlet Beauty is a Morton Arboretum selection bred for superior cold hardiness and vivid orange-red fall color.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; native Virginia sweetspire tolerates both boggy sites and average garden moisture once established. Scarlet Beauty, a Morton Arboretum introduction, was selected for exceptional cold hardiness beyond that of most Itea virginica cultivars and for vivid orange-red fall foliage color, following the fragrant, drooping white flower racemes typical of the species in early summer. Its shade and moisture tolerance make it a strong choice for a rain garden, pond edge, or low spot in a partly shaded border. Prune immediately after flowering if needed, since it blooms on old wood.

common_name: Suzanne Dwarf Fothergilla (True-Dwarf Fragrant Bottlebrush Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Suzanne is a true-dwarf Fothergilla selection reaching under two feet, well suited to small gardens.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; more sun exposure produces better fall color, but the shrub tolerates a good bit of shade. Suzanne stays notably compact, generally under two feet tall, making it one of the smallest Fothergilla selections available, yet still produces the species' signature fragrant white bottlebrush flower spikes in early spring before the leaves emerge, followed by blue-green summer foliage that turns brilliant shades of yellow, orange, and red in fall. Its diminutive size fits foundation plantings and small borders where full-sized Fothergilla would be too large. Prune only lightly to shape, since it needs little routine maintenance once established.

common_name: Downy Arrowwood (Native Understory Viburnum for Birds)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Downy Arrowwood is a native understory viburnum tolerant of dry shade beneath larger trees.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Downy Arrowwood tolerates dry shade beneath established trees better than most flowering shrubs, an unusually useful trait for a difficult woodland-edge site. Clusters of small white flowers open in late spring, followed by blue-black berries in fall that are quickly stripped by songbirds, while the soft, downy-textured leaves take on burgundy-red fall color. As a native understory shrub it supports a range of pollinators and birds, making it a valuable addition to a native woodland or hedgerow planting. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood, since it needs minimal maintenance once established.

common_name: Diane's Gold Brunnera (Chartreuse-Gold Heartleaf Shade Perennial)

planting.note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; Diane's Gold holds its chartreuse-gold heart-shaped foliage color through the summer better than many gold-leaved perennials.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade, protected from hot afternoon sun that can scorch the bright foliage. Diane's Gold bears bold, heart-shaped, chartreuse-gold leaves that hold their bright color through the summer better than many gold-leaved shade perennials, topped in early spring by sprays of small, sky-blue, forget-me-not-like flowers before the foliage fully expands. Its glowing foliage color lights up a dark corner of the garden long after the spring flowers fade. Keep soil consistently moist, especially during summer heat, and divide congested clumps in early spring or fall.

common_name: Variegata Brunnera (Classic Cream-Margined Heartleaf Bugloss)

planting.note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; Variegata is an older classic Brunnera selection with irregular cream-white leaf margins.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade, protected from hot afternoon sun that can scorch the variegated foliage. Variegata bears heart-shaped green leaves irregularly edged in creamy white, one of the older and longest-cultivated Brunnera variegated selections, topped in early spring by sprays of small, sky-blue, forget-me-not-like flowers before the foliage fully expands. Its bright, irregular leaf margins add textural contrast to a shaded planting alongside hostas and ferns. Keep soil consistently moist, especially during summer heat, and divide congested clumps in early spring or fall.

common_name: Bertram Anderson Lungwort (Narrow Silver-Spotted Blue-Flowered Pulmonaria)

planting.note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Bertram Anderson bears narrow, heavily silver-spotted leaves and vivid blue spring flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; consistent moisture prevents the leaves from wilting or scorching in summer heat. Bertram Anderson bears narrow, elongated leaves heavily marked with silver spots, a finer-textured look than many broader-leaved lungwort cultivars, topped in early spring by clusters of vivid blue flowers that open from pink-tinged buds. Its narrow foliage habit and strong flower color have kept it a long-standing favorite among Pulmonaria collectors. Cut back tattered summer foliage to encourage a fresh flush of clean new leaves, and divide congested clumps in fall.

common_name: Dream Weaver Hosta (Blue-Green Margin Cream-Center Hosta)

planting.note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Dream Weaver is a sport of Great Expectations with a wide blue-green margin around a creamy-white center.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; consistent moisture and protection from slugs keep the foliage looking its best through the season. Dream Weaver, a sport of the popular 'Great Expectations,' bears large, substantial leaves with a wide, irregular blue-green margin surrounding a bright creamy-white center, a bold two-tone pattern that brightens a shaded bed, topped in summer by pale lavender flowers on tall scapes. Its striking variegation and large leaf size make it a strong focal specimen among ferns and other shade perennials. Divide congested clumps in spring or fall, and apply slug bait or barriers if damage appears.

common_name: Herrenhausen Soft Shield Fern (Finely Divided Golden-Green Lacy Fern)

planting.note: Plant container-grown ferns in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; Herrenhausen bears finely divided, lacy golden-green fronds and tolerates more drought than most ferns once established.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; once established, this cultivar tolerates more drought than most ferns, though regular moisture keeps the fronds lushest. Herrenhausen forms an elegant, arching rosette of finely divided, lacy, golden-green fronds, a finer, more delicate texture than many other soft shield fern selections, holding its evergreen-to-semi-evergreen foliage through much of the winter in milder zones. Its refined, feathery texture makes it a graceful companion to bolder-leaved hostas and heucheras in a shaded border. Remove tattered old fronds in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in spring if needed.
